title: She Failed Her Child. She Kept The Ideology.
author: Peter Boghossian
summary: Peter Boghossian credits Nikole Hannah-Jones for admitting in the New York Times Magazine that her school choices harmed her daughter, but argues that she questions the cost without rethinking the cause. In his reading, she ranked a statistical child as more morally urgent than the child in her own house and still will not concede that ranking was wrong. He challenges her treatment of poverty and segregation as the mechanisms of failure, citing research showing poor white and Asian students outscoring poor Black students and a near-zero correlation between district spending and performance. He notes that the examples of bad teaching in her essay point to checked-out staff and weak instruction rather than wealth. Boghossian concludes that insisting Black schools need other races to succeed is itself a racist premise, pointing to successful majority-minority schools as counterexamples.
points: Boghossian argues Hannah-Jones concedes the harm to Najya while refusing to retire the ideology that produced it.
He describes her as leftist in valuing distant people over those nearby, yet conservative in acting on duties owed to community.
Poverty alone does not explain achievement gaps, since poor white and Asian students outscore poor Black students by wide margins.
The failures in her own account stem from poor instruction and disengaged staff, not a lack of money.
Vertex Partnership Academies and Michaela are cited as almost entirely minority schools that succeed.
quotes: Nikole Hannah-Jones, best known for creating The 1619 Project, concedes harm to her child yet still will not retire the ideology that caused the harm.

Jones does question the cost, but she does not rethink the cause. She treated a statistical child as more morally urgent than the child in her house. She will admit what that ranking cost Najya. She will not admit the ranking was wrong.
Jones treats “poor and black” as if poverty were the mechanism. It is not sufficient. Poor white and poor Asian students outscore poor black students by a wide margin.
Instead, it’s poor instruction and staff who don’t care and are checked out.
Jones writes as if a black school cannot succeed until enrollment racial demographics change. Why do black schools need white and Asian people to be successful?

What Jones does not do is shed the ideology that produced the harm. She still reads the wreckage as proof that segregated schools are the problem. Her ideology required a sacrificial child. The child noticed. The ideology did not.
